MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "osteoid osteoma"
- "Lateral X-ray of the tibia, physis **closed**: a **diaphyseal, cortical, osteosclerotic** lesion — a small **nidus** (<1.5 cm), **well-defined**."
- "The cortex shows **fusiform thickening** from reactive sclerosis; no destruction. So → **benign latent**."
- "Night pain relieved by aspirin → **osteoid osteoma**; differential Brodie abscess, stress fracture, osteoblastoma."
- "Next → **thin-cut CT (computed tomography)** for the nidus; bone scan if the X-ray is normal. Treatment → **CT-guided radiofrequency ablation (RFA)**."

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **10–35, male · cortical diaphysis, femur–tibia · nidus <1.5 cm + sclerosis · osteoblast-rimmed osteoid · NSAIDs → RFA**

### 1 Definition
- Osteoid osteoma → **benign latent**, bony origin (Handbook) · a small osteoid nidus in vascular stroma, ringed by reactive sclerosis
- Limited growth; **no malignant change ever documented** (Campbell)

### 2 Origin
- A true neoplasm: **FOS or FOSB** rearrangement, shared with osteoblastoma (Fittall 2018) · old theories → know only the **prostaglandin** story (Prof Abosena)

HIGH YIELD — why night pain, why aspirin
- Nidus makes **prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin** and holds **nerve endings**; night vasodilatation of the vascular nidus → more pain
- Aspirin and NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) block **COX-1 and COX-2** (cyclo-oxygenase) → prostaglandins fall → pain stops

### 3 Incidence
- Age **10–35**, peak second decade · **Sex** → **male : female 3 : 1** · **Relative incidence** → **10–12% of benign bone tumours** (OKU Tumors 4; Greenspan)

### 4 Sites
- **Longitudinal** → Diaphyseal (typical) · **Transverse** → **cortical** commonest; medullary, subperiosteal, intracapsular; rarely multifocal
- **Femur and tibia ≈50%**, femoral neck classic; **Special sites** → also hand, foot, talus · spine → **posterior elements**, mostly lumbar (OKU Tumors 4)

- Osteoid osteoma sites, age and sex, diagram (Greenspan)
Groups → **sclerotic lesions** of the young → 1 Differential (Prof Abosena) · no site is excluded: the Handbook's "never calcaneus" is wrong (Miller Fig 9-8)

- Four types: cortical, medullary, subperiosteal, intracapsular (Greenspan)
